brief.head: The British way of war
brief.text: Every military builds on a precondition, Ajay Shah said. For Britain it was overwhelming naval domination; for NATO today it is air superiority, which Russia never won over Ukraine. {029-C01}

brief.head: Hackers beat users
brief.text: Real excellence, Ajay Shah argued, comes from knowing your tools well enough to take them apart and rebuild them, as engineers did with the B-25 bomber. {029-C03}

brief.head: Drop, seize, hold on
brief.text: Paratroopers seize an airfield behind the lines and hold out for the main forces. In Crete it worked; at Arnhem, Ajay Shah said, the main forces never arrived. {029-C11}

brief.head: The invention of India
brief.text: India was not just discovered, as Nehru put it, Amit Varma said, but invented: a vision imposed on people who may not have wanted it. {029-J16}

brief.head: Uber for artillery
brief.text: Fighting for survival, Ukrainians innovated wherever they could not get things done, Amit Varma said, even building an Uber for artillery in the middle of a war. {029-J19}

lead.kicker: Varma and Shah pitch five stories for the screen
lead.head: Lights, camera, history
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah came with five stories that, they argued, should be films: three told by Shah and two by Varma, alternating so that Shah went first and last. {#threetwo}
They had done a show like it before. Pieces of history like these, Shah said, could be a movie, should be a movie, and at worst were a great story that “gentle reader shall suffer from us”.
The canvases were vast: the fall of France, the war in the Pacific, the birth of independent India, the battle for Kiev. Yet every pitch came back to one person facing one problem.

Varma put the principle in a sentence about his own story: “A macrocosm of ideological zeal and one way of looking at the world coming to a fall can also contain the microcosm of the relationship of these people.” {029-C07}
## Five pitches
Shah opened in the summer of 1940, at the Algerian port of Mers-el-Kébir, where Churchill ordered the Royal Navy to destroy the French fleet rather than let it fall to Germany.
Varma followed with a fiction laid over fact: ERP, an AT&T outfit that preached clean cinema sound to the world, and a married couple inside it who begin to hear rooms differently.
Shah’s second pitch was the Doolittle Raid of April 1942, in which hacked American bombers flew off a carrier, struck Japan and headed on for China.
Varma’s second was the making of independent India, seen through VP Menon, the bureaucrat at Sardar Patel’s side, who as a schoolboy had burned down his school.
Shah closed with the battle of Kiev in 2022, and Volodymyr Zelensky, the comedian president who would not leave.
## Why war makes cinema

Shah admitted that some of his stories are just things that blow up. But the Second World War, he said, holds the mind for a deeper reason: “Because the fate of the world is on the line. The stakes are sky high.” {029-C08}
The Falklands had dramatic moments, he said, but nobody wants that film: the stakes were so low, “like academic politics”. Varma held that any story with humans in it has high stakes.
## No easy endings
Several pitches had no Hollywood resolution. Of Mers-el-Kébir, Varma said: “There is no victory for anyone. There is a deep moral dilemma and a sense of unease and nothing is resolved.”
Shah’s caution against verdicts: “So hindsight is easy. What’s really, really difficult is standing there.” {029-C02}
The same unease ran through Varma’s India. He loves the country, he said, but feels deep disquiet that it was assembled from more than 500 princely states through coercion and broken promises.
“The moment you say that the end justifies a means,” he said, “then you can make up any end in your head.” And then, he added, you can commit the greatest brutality. {029-C09}
Small accidents mattered too. A stranger’s ten rupees to a penniless young Menon, Varma suggested, may have changed the course of India.

The hosts closed with recommendations. Varma chose David Byrne’s *How Music Works*, “the best book I’ve ever read about music”; Shah chose the YouTube channel of William Spaniel, for some of the best understanding of the battle of Kiev as it unfolded.

second.label: The princely states
second.head: Every dog accounted for
second.deck: Amit Varma on the Nawab of Junagadh’s flight to Karachi, and his priorities
body: As India was being put together after independence, the Nawab of Junagadh realised he had to go. {029-S07} Amit Varma told what happened next as a scene from a film.
A plane was chartered. Into it went the treasury, the jewellery, his dogs, his begums and his children. As it was about to take off, one begum cried that her child was still in the palace.

The Nawab looked around and counted the dogs. All the dogs were there. “I love you, it was nice knowing you. Please get off,” he told her, in Varma’s telling. She got off, and the plane left for Karachi. With 547 princely states, “or whatever they were”, Varma said, there were 547 such stories. {#stories}

quote.text: And he looks around, and he counts the dogs, and all the dogs are there

second.caption: the Nawab of Junagadh’s dogs

third.head: Ride a bike like a bat
body: What if, Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma, you could learn to echolocate like a bat? Varma asked if he was kidding. “I’m dead serious,” Shah said.

Take people who lost their sight after about the age of five, once they had learnt to see. With careful training, Shah said, two-thirds of them can orient themselves the way bats do, whistling and listening for the echoes. “This is the power that resides inside each of us. We are just not aware of it.” {029-C05}
Some, he said, ride bicycles outdoors this way, sensing traffic and houses. {029-S03}

Varma brought a data point against, Thomas Nagel’s essay *What Is It Like to Be a Bat?*, and one in favour: a visually impaired colleague of Krish Ashok’s who listens to everything at six times speed. {#sixx}
third.caption: learning to echolocate

p2.title: Coming attractions
p2.deck: Five stories the hosts believe should be films, and what each says about history, judgement and people

sections.label: Pitch One
sections.head: Sinking a friend’s fleet
sections.caption: the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir
body: In the summer of 1940, Ajay Shah said, Rommel’s tanks blasted through the Ardennes and France signed an armistice. What, then, of the French Navy, which by default would fall into German hands?

For Britain that was intolerable. In the British way of war, Shah said, the Royal Navy would always have “a ridiculous level of domination on the seas”, just as American and NATO doctrine today begins with air superiority. {029-C01}
Britain had landed some 300,000 men in France to fight alongside the French. {#expeditionary} Now it asked the French Navy, through informal channels, to bring its ships over.
## Pride and obedience

Three things pulled the French the other way, Shah said: orders from Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime, a military culture of blind obedience, and a belief that France was a first-class power, even a Vishwaguru.
Some French officers promised to scuttle the ships if the Germans came for them. But that, Shah said, was a promise about a future event.
At Mers-el-Kébir the Royal Navy pleaded until the very end. The French refused, Churchill gave the order, and about 1,300 sailors died. {029-S01}
Churchill wrote that it was one of the worst decisions he had to make in the war. Some historians call it a mistake; Shah sides with Churchill.
~ Amit Varma saw a film needing Hollywood scale with no Hollywood ending. Shah’s reply to the urge to judge was simple: hindsight is easy, standing there is hard. {029-C02}

quote.text: So in that one decision, Churchill created the death of thirteen hundred French soldiers who really were not Nazi Germany.

sections.label: Pitch Two
sections.head: Hearing each other out
sections.caption: the couple who heard differently
body: Amit Varma’s first pitch was half fact, half fiction. The fact was ERP, the AT&T unit that preached clean sound to cinemas across the world from 1926. The fiction was a marriage. His working title: *Silence of the Heart*.
In his story a couple join ERP together, the way a couple might join a religious cult or a physics lab. Part of their love is a shared passion.

Then the woman starts to hear rooms differently from her husband and the other ERP men. At first, Varma said, she gaslights herself: something must be wrong with her ears. Later she owns it. Why is he right? Why is she wrong?
## A film for the ears
Everyone in a room hears it differently, Varma argued, without being able to say so. “And in this hearing there is also a metaphor for the ways in which you see the world differently.” {029-C06}
Films often show couples drifting apart because they see the world differently, he said. He could not think of one about a couple drifting apart because they hear it differently. {029-S02}

~ Ajay Shah proposed a separate filter for each partner’s landscape, “something that is perceptible in Dolby Audio”. {#dolby} He called it a nice feminist film. Varma preferred to call it a human story.

quote.text: But imagine two people drifting apart because they hear the world differently.

sections.label: Pitch Three
sections.head: The plane nobody imagined
sections.caption: the hacked B-25 bomber
body: After Pearl Harbor, Ajay Shah said, America wanted to hit Japan itself, to disrupt a formidable production machine and to puncture the complacency of a people fed propaganda about their first strike.
Japan was out of reach. So engineers hacked the B-25 bomber in sixteen different ways, adding de-icing gear and fuel tanks for perhaps 80 or 90 per cent more range. {#sixteen}
Shah drew a lesson for everyone: “You can be a dumb user of other people’s creations, or you can know enough about them that you’re able to take it apart and modify it”. {029-C03}
## A failure of imagination

When a Japanese ship sighted the carrier group and radioed home, Japan prepared for a sea battle. Nobody there could imagine bombers taking off from a carrier, hitting Japan and flying on to China. {029-C04}
Amit Varma’s diagnosis: someone was naval gazing, not navel gazing. “He was fighting the last war, so to speak,” said Shah. {029-J04}
~ Varma saw the film in its human moments: crews told to take off early, not knowing if they would come back, driven by duty, “even though your commander is a guy called Doolittle.” {029-J03}

quote.text: But the interesting thing that happened on the Japanese side was the failure of imagination.

portraits.hint: American airman who led the raid

sections.label: Pitch Four
sections.head: Stitched, not discovered
sections.caption: the making of independent India
body: Amit Varma loves India, he said, and is glad he can go from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. But he feels deep disquiet about how it was put together.

At independence there were more than 500 princely states, 327 of them, he thought, really small. {#princely} In two or three years Sardar Patel and VP Menon built them into today’s map, by means that included coercion and broken promises.

Once you say the end justifies the means, he argued, you can make up any end and commit the greatest brutality. {029-C09} He calls it fast-track colonisation: what the British did over two or three hundred years, Patel and Menon did in a couple of years.
Offstage, cats began screaming, “because they get the sense of what I am saying”, he said. {029-J08}
## What if
Ajay Shah had his own counterfactuals. What if India had not taken over Goa, now perhaps part of the European Union? {#goa} What if the British had kept Surat as India’s Hong Kong?

Varma imagined many small states, too weak to fight but competing to govern well. Shah doubted it: the princely states had very poor political development, with nothing like England’s path from the Magna Carta in 1215. {#magna}
~ The world is this way, Varma said, because of a series of accidents. It could have been a million different things.

quote.text: Imagine if there was a bit of a Hong Kong in India. What if the British had kept Surat?

sections.label: Pitch Five
sections.head: The comedian stays put
sections.caption: the battle of Kiev
body: In 2022, Ajay Shah said, the supposedly second most powerful army in the world smashed into Ukraine, a messy country with weak institutions. “Ukraine is like India,” he said.
Its president, Volodymyr Zelensky, was a television comedian who had once played the president of Ukraine in a show in which Russia invades. Many expected him to flee, as Afghanistan’s leaders had.

He stayed, though early on there was an assassination attempt against him every day. {#assassination} He was no hero, he later said, only a man who knew that if he left, everything would collapse. {029-S08}
## Blind, but warned

Russian cyberwarfare knocked out government communications, and officials talked on WhatsApp. {#whatsapp} But Russians inside Putin’s system had leaked the invasion plans, and key defence assets were moved, so the first strikes hit empty sites.

Russian paratroopers took Hostomel airport, as the CIA director Burns had foreseen. Then the Ukrainians mounted a scrappy underdog defence, even blowing up a bridge to flood a Russian route of attack. {#bridge}
~ The Russians withdrew from the Kiev region. Amit Varma recalled Zelensky’s answer to an American offer to get him out: “I don’t want a ride, I want ammo.” {029-J13}

quote.text: Actually, I was just a scared, terrified guy standing in the gun sights, making a call every minute, every hour about what to do.
quote.who: Volodymyr Zelensky, in Ajay Shah’s telling

side.boxText: Zoom in, Amit Varma said: a macrocosm, like ERP’s zeal rising and falling, can contain a microcosm, like a marriage. Ajay Shah’s test was the stakes: individual life and death, with the fate of the world on the line. {029-C08}

contQuote.text: And it strikes me that in this age we kinda have to do both. That you have both the first draft of history and the sense making happening simultaneously.

p3.title: Now showing
p3.deck: Four tellings from the episode, and the lesson behind each

stories.start: there is a boy in a school in the early nineteen hundreds
stories.end: everybody can't go out and rebel. And he stays within the system.
stories.caption: VP Menon’s schoolboy fire
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on VP Menon’s origin story, in scattered scenes
stories.head: Cold lunch, then the matchbox
body: Amit Varma pitched it as a story told in scattered scenes. In the early 1900s a schoolboy is failed in his examination for poor attendance. He tries to explain how far he has to come; the teacher will not hear it. He runs out in tears, grabbing his lunchbox.

He sits shaking at a railway station where he likes to read. He walks by the river. Under a tree he eats his cold lunch and falls asleep as the light changes. He wakes at dusk beside an empty liquor bottle some drunkard has left.
At a liquor shop he buys something that looks like a bottle, saying his mother will pay later. Then he asks for a matchbox. The last scene: the school is on fire.
The boy was VP Menon. He fled by train to Kolar, and decades later could still name every station on the way. {#stations}
In the Kolar mines he was soon giving orders to men twice his age. {#mines} Then he sold towels on the streets of Bombay.

In Delhi he stepped off the train to find his pocket picked. A Sardarji stranger gave him ten rupees, a huge sum then, and Menon forgot to ask his name. “If that little event doesn’t happen, India could be in a different place,” Varma said. {029-S05}

~ Menon joined the government as a clerk, nearly quit after the Rowlatt Act, and then decided that some people must stay within the system to change it. {#rowlatt} He became Sardar Patel’s executor in bringing in the princely states.
stories.why: Behind the “expressionless bureaucrat” was a complex man, Varma said, for whom work was a mission but who was bad with his wife and children. And behind the making of India lie tiny accidents, like a stranger’s ten rupees. {#tenbucks}
stories.postscript: Varma’s source is Narayani Basu’s *VP Menon: The Unsung Architect of Modern India*. Basu, he thinks, is Menon’s granddaughter. {029-R05}

stories.start: My second story starts uh at the attack on Pearl Harbor
stories.end: changed the psychological landscape in Japan that we're not getting away with this cheaply
stories.caption: the Doolittle Raid
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the raid that shook Japan in April 1942
stories.head: Take off early, land nowhere
body: After Pearl Harbor, Ajay Shah said, America wanted to strike Japan itself, though it was out of reach. The answer: B-25 bombers that could take off from a carrier but not land on one. They would fly on to China, where Chiang Kai-shek’s Kuomintang prepared airfields; Stalin had refused them Vladivostok because of his peace treaty with Japan. {#vladivostok}

A Japanese ship sighted the group and radioed home. The bombers took off early, from the wrong spot, hit their targets with reasonable success and fell short of China. Most crews were rescued by the Kuomintang. One plane landed at Vladivostok; the NKVD later staged its crew’s escape to Iran.
The raid came four months after Pearl Harbor, and it ended Japan’s sense of ease, Shah said. {029-S04}
~ Bystanders paid: Japan’s reprisal killed some 70,000 Chinese soldiers and 250,000 civilians. {#reprisal}

quote.text: And suddenly it changed the psychological landscape in Japan that we’re not getting away with this cheaply.

stories.start: There is one uh uh you know memorable scene which happens
stories.end: I'll make you win. And VP Minan, of course, says no.
stories.caption: the Maharaja of Jodhpur’s pen-gun
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a prince, a pen and VP Menon’s nerve
stories.head: The pen was also a gun
body: Hanwant Singh, the Maharaja of Jodhpur, was being courted by Pakistan. “Jinnah offered me a blank cheque,” he told VP Menon and Mountbatten, in Amit Varma’s telling. {#jodhpurblank}
On paper, Varma said, the princes could join India or Pakistan or stay independent. In practice independence was never possible, and a state inside India could not go to Pakistan.

They persuaded him at last. Mountbatten left the room, and as Hanwant Singh was about to sign, he pointed his pen at Menon. The pen was also a gun. {#pengun} In Varma’s cinematic imagining, Menon raises an eyebrow and smiles, and the Maharaja signs. {029-S06}
~ Years later Hanwant Singh offered to make Menon the MP from Jodhpur. Menon said no. {#jodhpurmp}
stories.why: India’s map was not drawn calmly. It was negotiated one prince at a time, with coercion where needed and persuasion where possible, Varma said; and every princely state had a story like this one. {#stories}

stories.start: So in nineteen twenty six, ATT set up a department called ERP
stories.end: landscape of sound, as it were, changes both people the way that they hear
stories.caption: ERP’s sound evangelists
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on AT&T’s crusade for clean cinema sound
stories.head: Crusaders against the echo
body: In 1926, Amit Varma said, AT&T set up Electrical Research Products Incorporated, ERP, to evangelise sound in cinemas across the world. Its men carried kits, listened for echoes and fixed rooms with padding and drapes.

David Byrne, in *How Music Works*, pictures uniformed men communicating through hand signals and perfect silence, “like some acoustic Sherlock Holmes”. {029-J14} Yet in Canton, Ohio, they were baffled by a gentle roar near the screen, until they found six caged lions from a nearby circus behind the stage. {#lions}
ERP went from about 1,000 screens at the start of 1929 to 4,000 by its end. {#screens} But the French burned a theatre down, and India mastered sound and told ERP it was not needed. {#indians}
~ Onto this history Varma laid a fiction: a husband and wife in ERP who begin to hear rooms differently. {029-S02}
stories.why: In France and India, Varma said, ERP’s cultural, almost moral mission met its match. It had set out to spread its values everywhere, “almost like an American version of Macaulay”. {029-J15}
stories.postscript: ERP’s newsletter, Varma added, was called ERPigram.

quiz.q: Where did the Royal Navy destroy the French fleet in 1940, killing about 1,300 sailors?
quiz.a: At the Algerian port of Mers-el-Kébir, on Winston Churchill’s order.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s imagined ERP film, why does the married couple drift apart?
quiz.a: Because the woman starts hearing rooms differently from her husband and everyone else.

quiz.q: What share of people who lost their sight after about age five can learn echolocation, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: About two-thirds; some even ride bicycles outdoors by whistling and listening.

quiz.q: Why did Japan fail to anticipate the Doolittle Raid after spotting the American carrier group?
quiz.a: A failure of imagination: nobody thought a carrier plane could reach Japan.

quiz.q: What did a Sardarji stranger give VP Menon at Delhi station, and what did Menon forget?
quiz.a: Ten rupees, a fortune then; Menon forgot to ask the man’s name.

quiz.q: What did Zelensky say when the Americans offered to get him out of Ukraine?
quiz.a: “I don’t want a ride, I want ammo”, as Amit Varma recounted it.
